can solve that problem, but only when the programme is designed as a regulated billing operation, not treated as an equipment purchase. This guide tells you where the friction lives and what to demand before signing an agreement.

Why Landlords Are Turning to Electric Submetering in 2026

Master-metered buildings hide consumption differences. A quiet suite, a vacant unit, and a resident who runs high-load equipment can sit inside the same bulk electricity charge. The owner absorbs the variation, subsidises usage that should be recoverable, and faces a difficult conversation whenever a tenant questions a shared allocation.

Unit-level billing can recover consumption that owners previously carried, including power used in occupied suites, vacant spaces, and areas that need separate treatment. It also gives managers a defensible record when a resident asks how a charge was calculated.

Transparent consumption data can support operating-budget decisions and help owners separate tenant loads from common-area loads. electricity consumption reduction guidance

Regulatory and Compliance Checks Before You Sign
The first question isn't which meter a salesperson recommends. It's whether your property can legally use the proposed submetering and billing model.

In Ontario, the OEB says a person may not engage in unit sub-metering without the required licence under section 57(c.1) of the Ontario Energy Board Act, 1998. The OEB Unit Sub-Metering Code also governs operational requirements, including installation, testing, reading, maintenance, and billing-related processes such as validating, estimating, and editing metering data. A licensed provider must be able to show how its workflow addresses those obligations, not just provide a hardware brochure.
Ontario's code requires a
minimum payment period of 20 days for submetered bills

. Build that requirement into your billing calendar from the beginning. The landlord or operator also needs a clear account structure with the local distributor, documented meter assignments, and records that support every bill issued.

Measurement Canada adds another layer. Electricity meters used in transactions must meet applicable accuracy and approval requirements, so ask for the exact meter model, approval documentation, sealing approach, and post-installation verification process. Don't accept “revenue grade” as a complete answer. That phrase doesn't replace the approval and inspection evidence relevant to your property.
Practical rule:
If a vendor can't show its licence position, meter approval path, billing controls, and record-retention process before contract signing, pause the project.
Jurisdiction changes the answer

Outside Ontario, the rules can change by state, property type, utility arrangement, and billing method. California is a clear example. California commercial energy submetering guidance
before treating submetering as a standard cost-recovery measure.

Choosing the Right Equipment and Service Model
The wrong equipment creates recurring service calls. The wrong contract leaves the landlord responsible for data, billing corrections, and replacement decisions that seemed minor during procurement.

Start with the electrical panel. Single-phase and three-phase loads need different designs. Indoor panels, exterior enclosures, damp areas, and mechanically crowded rooms each impose different installation requirements.

Communications deserve equal attention. Hardwired systems can be dependable in buildings with accessible pathways, but pulling cable through occupied suites increases coordination. Wireless mesh can simplify retrofits, though signal surveys and gateway placement matter. Cellular gateways reduce dependence on the building's IT network. Power-line carrier systems can use existing electrical infrastructure, but interference and circuit topology need testing.

and ask the vendor to identify every landlord-side dependency.

Tenant Communication and Billing in Practice

Consider a six-suite triplex with a master electricity meter and separate suite submeters. The property manager has an older adult resident in unit 3, so the billing rollout needs to be clear, accessible, and easy to challenge without forcing the resident to interpret raw technical data.

The meters send raw pulse or interval information to the billing platform. The platform validates the readings, checks for gaps or abnormal changes, maps each meter to the correct unit, and applies the approved billing methodology. The resident should receive a readable PDF, not an unexplained export from a meter database.
What the invoice must show

A clean invoice identifies the unit, billing period, opening and closing reads, consumption, rate calculation, applicable charges, and a contact route for questions. For Ontario programmes, the payment period must not compress below the
20-day minimum
required by the OEB Unit Sub-Metering Code, as noted in the regulatory guidance above.

Don't promise residents a “fair bill” without defining fairness operationally. It means the correct meter serves the correct suite, the reading interval is valid, the rate is applied consistently, and the invoice contains enough information for a reasonable person to understand the result.
Disputes need a controlled workflow

A resident may report an unexpectedly high bill, a suspected meter fault, or a mismatch between their occupancy and the charge. The property manager should log the inquiry, preserve the original invoice, check the meter status, review the interval data, and rerun the calculation if a sensor or communications point is flagged.

A six-suite building is small enough for a manager to know the residents personally, but that doesn't justify informal adjustments. Use a documented correction process. If the data is estimated, mark it as estimated, explain why, and issue a corrected bill after validation.

The invoice should also distinguish unit electricity from common-area electricity where the programme includes both. That separation helps the owner understand building performance and prevents residents from assuming that a suite charge includes every load on the property.
Long-Term Service, Data, and Maintenance

The service agreement matters more than the initial hardware quote because the meters will remain part of the building's operating system for years. A low upfront price can become expensive if every failed read, tenant inquiry, firmware issue, and export request becomes a separate charge.

Owners usually underestimate three obligations. First, electricity meters may require ongoing seal and accuracy verification under the applicable Measurement Canada pathway. Second, gateways and communications systems need firmware, cellular, Wi-Fi, or network administration. Third, the billing platform needs a retention policy that matches the landlord's legal, accounting, dispute, and asset-management requirements.
Put ownership in writing

The raw interval data should belong to the property owner or be available to the owner without restrictive export terms. Require practical formats, complete historical records, meter metadata, unit mappings, and billing files. Data should be usable for benchmarking, capital planning, equipment troubleshooting, and resident dispute reviews.

Ask what happens if the vendor is sold, changes platforms, stops supporting a meter model, or loses a communications carrier. The contract should define transition assistance, data delivery, account access, and responsibility for equipment during the handover.
Owners who want broader visibility can also review resources on how to
track your home energy usage
. The same principle applies at building scale: measurement is useful only when people can access, interpret, and act on the data.
Budget for recurring work

Wireless models may need battery replacement. Gateways may need service or replacement. Software licences can renew separately from hardware support. Meter accuracy checks, tenant-billing administration, and field visits all belong in the operating budget from day one.
A commissioned system is not a finished system. It is a service obligation with data, maintenance, compliance, and resident-support requirements.

Build an annual review into the management calendar. Check meter exceptions, estimated reads, open disputes, communications outages, export integrity, replacement stock, and invoice samples. That review catches programme drift before a small configuration problem becomes a portfolio-wide billing issue.
Landlord Action Checklist and Common Questions
Give the property manager a sequence they can execute, with an owner sign-off at every control point. The following checklist is designed for that handoff.
Complete the regulatory pre-check.
Confirm the property type, province or state, utility structure, licensing trigger, disclosure rules, and permitted charges.
Verify the vendor.
Check licence status, insurance, electrical qualifications, meter approvals, commissioning procedures, data ownership, and exit terms.
Confirm the account structure.
Verify that the utility customer of record, master meter, distributor relationship, and common-area loads are correctly documented.
Review the lease rider.
Have counsel approve the billing methodology, rate language, dispute route, notice requirements, and any applicable fee treatment.
Issue tenant notice.
Provide the required written notice, explain access needs, describe the billing change plainly, and offer a contact route for questions.
Sign off installation.
Match serial numbers to suites, confirm panel assignments, retain photographs and test records, and close every access exception.
Approve billing go-live.
Run a dry cycle, compare readings, review invoice fields, test corrections, and release bills only after approval.
Audit the first three cycles.
Sample invoices, review estimates and exceptions, check the master-meter reconciliation, and log resident disputes.
Review annually.
Confirm service performance, data exports, accuracy checks, communications health, contract renewals, and replacement planning.

children.text: Common questions landlords ask
What happens when a meter fails?
The billing system should flag missing or suspect data, apply the approved estimation process where permitted, and document the correction. Don't substitute a number.
Who pays for replacement?
Your agreement should say whether ordinary failure, vandalism, obsolescence, and installation labour are included. If it doesn't, assume the issue will become a dispute.
How are vacant suites billed?
Follow the lease, tenancy law, and the approved billing methodology. A vacant unit isn't a reason to transfer an undocumented charge to other residents.
Can tenants refuse?
Access and billing rights depend on the jurisdiction, lease, notice, and property type. Confirm the legal position before issuing appointment notices.
How are rate caps enforced?

Configure the billing platform with the approved rate rules, retain the source tariff, and review invoices during the first cycles. California's 2025 guidance specifically highlights itemised readings, service rates, and administrative fees as part of transparent submetered billing.
What records must the landlord retain?

Keep licences, meter approvals, commissioning results, serial-number mappings, reads, invoices, corrections, notices, tariffs, dispute records, and vendor service reports for the period required by applicable law and your own risk policy.

Whole-building read Supports reconciliation with the master account Utility master meter
Allocator or calculation method Explains how the charge was derived Approved billing configuration
Rate and fee disclosure Separates the energy rate and permitted charges Utility tariff, lease, and applicable rules

Don't promise residents a “fair bill” without defining fairness operationally. It means the correct meter serves the correct suite, the reading interval is valid, the rate is applied consistently, and the invoice contains enough information for a reasonable person to understand the result.

Disputes need a controlled workflow

A resident may report an unexpectedly high bill, a suspected meter fault, or a mismatch between their occupancy and the charge. The property manager should log the inquiry, preserve the original invoice, check the meter status, review the interval data, and rerun the calculation if a sensor or communications point is flagged.

A six-suite building is small enough for a manager to know the residents personally, but that doesn't justify informal adjustments. Use a documented correction process. If the data is estimated, mark it as estimated, explain why, and issue a corrected bill after validation.

The invoice should also distinguish unit electricity from common-area electricity where the programme includes both. That separation helps the owner understand building performance and prevents residents from assuming that a suite charge includes every load on the property.

Long-Term Service, Data, and Maintenance

The service agreement matters more than the initial hardware quote because the meters will remain part of the building's operating system for years. A low upfront price can become expensive if every failed read, tenant inquiry, firmware issue, and export request becomes a separate charge.

Owners usually underestimate three obligations. First, electricity meters may require ongoing seal and accuracy verification under the applicable Measurement Canada pathway. Second, gateways and communications systems need firmware, cellular, Wi-Fi, or network administration. Third, the billing platform needs a retention policy that matches the landlord's legal, accounting, dispute, and asset-management requirements.

Put ownership in writing

The raw interval data should belong to the property owner or be available to the owner without restrictive export terms. Require practical formats, complete historical records, meter metadata, unit mappings, and billing files. Data should be usable for benchmarking, capital planning, equipment troubleshooting, and resident dispute reviews.

Ask what happens if the vendor is sold, changes platforms, stops supporting a meter model, or loses a communications carrier. The contract should define transition assistance, data delivery, account access, and responsibility for equipment during the handover.

Owners who want broader visibility can also review resources on how to track your home energy usage. The same principle applies at building scale: measurement is useful only when people can access, interpret, and act on the data.

Budget for recurring work

Wireless models may need battery replacement. Gateways may need service or replacement. Software licences can renew separately from hardware support. Meter accuracy checks, tenant-billing administration, and field visits all belong in the operating budget from day one.

A commissioned system is not a finished system. It is a service obligation with data, maintenance, compliance, and resident-support requirements.

Build an annual review into the management calendar. Check meter exceptions, estimated reads, open disputes, communications outages, export integrity, replacement stock, and invoice samples. That review catches programme drift before a small configuration problem becomes a portfolio-wide billing issue.

Landlord Action Checklist and Common Questions

Give the property manager a sequence they can execute, with an owner sign-off at every control point. The following checklist is designed for that handoff.

  1. Complete the regulatory pre-check. Confirm the property type, province or state, utility structure, licensing trigger, disclosure rules, and permitted charges.
  2. Verify the vendor. Check licence status, insurance, electrical qualifications, meter approvals, commissioning procedures, data ownership, and exit terms.
  3. Confirm the account structure. Verify that the utility customer of record, master meter, distributor relationship, and common-area loads are correctly documented.
  4. Review the lease rider. Have counsel approve the billing methodology, rate language, dispute route, notice requirements, and any applicable fee treatment.
  5. Issue tenant notice. Provide the required written notice, explain access needs, describe the billing change plainly, and offer a contact route for questions.
  6. Sign off installation. Match serial numbers to suites, confirm panel assignments, retain photographs and test records, and close every access exception.
  7. Approve billing go-live. Run a dry cycle, compare readings, review invoice fields, test corrections, and release bills only after approval.
  8. Audit the first three cycles. Sample invoices, review estimates and exceptions, check the master-meter reconciliation, and log resident disputes.
  9. Review annually. Confirm service performance, data exports, accuracy checks, communications health, contract renewals, and replacement planning.

Common questions landlords ask

What happens when a meter fails? The billing system should flag missing or suspect data, apply the approved estimation process where permitted, and document the correction. Don't substitute a number.

Who pays for replacement? Your agreement should say whether ordinary failure, vandalism, obsolescence, and installation labour are included. If it doesn't, assume the issue will become a dispute.

How are vacant suites billed? Follow the lease, tenancy law, and the approved billing methodology. A vacant unit isn't a reason to transfer an undocumented charge to other residents.

Can tenants refuse? Access and billing rights depend on the jurisdiction, lease, notice, and property type. Confirm the legal position before issuing appointment notices.

How are rate caps enforced? Configure the billing platform with the approved rate rules, retain the source tariff, and review invoices during the first cycles. California's 2025 guidance specifically highlights itemised readings, service rates, and administrative fees as part of transparent submetered billing.

What records must the landlord retain? Keep licences, meter approvals, commissioning results, serial-number mappings, reads, invoices, corrections, notices, tariffs, dispute records, and vendor service reports for the period required by applicable law and your own risk policy.
